past_medical_history: Chronic heavy alcohol use disorder (daily heavy drinker)

medications.indication: alcohol-related thiamine prophylaxis (prescribed 3 months ago, inconsistent adherence)

social_history.alcohol: 8-10 beers per day for >15 years; admits daily drinking since 20s

patient.chief_complaint: Bilateral burning foot pain, weakness, and difficulty walking — 2 years of progressive symptoms
patient.history_present_illness: A 56-year-old unemployed former construction worker with chronic heavy alcohol use disorder (8-10 beers per day for over 15 years) and malnutrition presented to the outpatient neurology clinic for evaluation of progressive bilateral foot pain and weakness over the past two years. He describes a constant burning sensation in both feet that started approximately two years ago, initially just at the soles, but now extending up to the mid-calf. The pain is severe enough to interfere with sleep and prevent him from wearing shoes comfortably. He has noticed progressive weakness in both legs — he trips frequently and has had three falls in the past six months. His gait has become increasingly unsteady. He has also noted loss of sensation in both hands over the past eight months — his grip is weaker than it used to be and he frequently drops objects. He lives alone and eats primarily fast food, rarely consuming vegetables, fruits, or protein-rich foods. He was prescribed thiamine three months ago but admits to taking it 'sometimes.' He denies headache, diplopia, confusion, or ataxia of the upper extremities. He has not seen a doctor regularly. On direct questioning he endorses significant proximal leg weakness — he has difficulty climbing stairs and rising from low chairs. He appears malnourished at examination — cachectic with temporal wasting.

neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert. Oriented x3. Mildly slowed processing. Memory intact. No Wernicke features (no ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, or confusion at this time).
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Normal. PERRL. No ophthalmoplegia. Horizontal gaze saccades normal.
neurological_exam.motor: Bilateral distal foot/toe weakness (EHL 3/5, ankle dorsiflexion 3+/5). Knee extension 4/5 bilaterally. Hip flexion 4/5. Upper extremities: mild bilateral intrinsic hand weakness (4/5 grip). No proximal upper extremity weakness.
neurological_exam.sensory: Severe bilateral stocking sensory loss to knees — light touch, pinprick, temperature, and vibration severely impaired. Bilateral glove sensory loss to mid-forearm. Proprioception reduced at bilateral great toes.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Ankle reflexes absent bilaterally. Knee jerks 1+ bilaterally. Biceps and brachioradialis 1+. Plantar flexors bilaterally.
neurological_exam.coordination: Marked sensory ataxia on heel-shin. Finger-nose mildly clumsy (sensory).
neurological_exam.gait: Wide-based steppage gait. Cannot walk on heels. Romberg markedly positive. Unable to tandem walk.
neurological_exam.additional: Cachectic appearance. Temporal muscle wasting. Spider angiomata on chest. Palmar erythema. Dupuytren's contracture early right hand.

labs.interpretation: Abnormal values: Hemoglobin 10.4 g/dL (L), MCV 108 fL (H), Platelets 96 x10^9/L (L), Sodium 134 mmol/L (L), Potassium 3.2 mmol/L (L), ALT 88 U/L (H), AST 128 U/L (H), GGT 342 U/L (H), Total bilirubin 1.8 mg/dL (H), Albumin 2.8 g/dL (L), Thiamine (B1) 28 nmol/L (L), Folate (serum) 1.8 ng/mL (L).

findings.pattern: Severely reduced amplitude, prolonged DML — axonal with secondary demyelination
Reduced — upper extremity involvement, glove pattern

emg_findings.comment: Proximal involvement suggests length-dependent + nutritional/toxic neuropathy

quantitative_data.pattern: Severe length-dependent axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy, severe — distal > proximal

specialized_test.impression: Severe length-dependent axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy. NCS shows absent or near-absent SNAP amplitudes bilaterally in lower extremities, severely reduced motor CMAPs. EMG shows severe chronic active denervation — proximal lower extremity involvement suggests a superimposed nutritional component beyond purely length-dependent disease. Pattern is consistent with alcoholic-nutritional polyneuropathy with thiamine deficiency as dominant mechanism.
recommended_actions: High-dose IV thiamine IMMEDIATELY — severe thiamine deficiency with Wernicke risk
IV thiamine 500 mg three times daily for 3-5 days, then oral maintenance

results.title: Wernicke encephalopathy — diagnosis and thiamine treatment protocol
results.key_finding: Classic triad present in only 16% of cases; IV thiamine 500 mg TID for 5 days recommended for any at-risk patient; MUST give thiamine before glucose infusions to prevent precipitating Wernicke

results.title: Thiamine blood levels and neuropathy in alcoholism
results.key_finding: Thiamine <40 nmol/L strongly associated with Wernicke-Korsakoff risk; neurological manifestations may be solely the peripheral neuropathy before central Wernicke develops

output.summary: Thiamine 28 nmol/L is critically low — Wernicke encephalopathy risk is high. IV thiamine 500 mg three times daily for 3-5 days is required urgently. This should be administered regardless of whether the classic Wernicke triad is present. NEVER give glucose without thiamine first in thiamine-deficient patients — precipitates acute Wernicke.

output.proposed: Alcohol cessation pharmacotherapy (naltrexone or acamprosate) for chronic alcohol use disorder
contraindications: Naltrexone — contraindicated if active hepatitis (AST 128, ALT 88 — caution; naltrexone relatively contraindicated with active hepatic inflammation, AST 3x ULN)
warnings: Naltrexone relatively contraindicated given elevated LFTs (AST 128 = 3.2x ULN)
Acamprosate is renally cleared — can be used with liver disease
Benzodiazepine taper required for alcohol withdrawal monitoring — CIWA protocol
alternatives: Acamprosate 666 mg TID (no hepatic metabolism — preferred with liver disease)
Gabapentin for alcohol withdrawal management may also help neuropathic pain

findings.finding: Echogenic liver consistent with alcoholic fatty liver/hepatitis. Spleen enlarged at 14 cm (splenomegaly). No ascites. No hepatocellular mass.

output.impression: Alcoholic hepatitis with splenomegaly (portal hypertension). No evidence of HCC. Hepatology referral required for liver disease staging and management.

results.title: Treatment of alcoholic peripheral neuropathy
results.key_finding: Thiamine (B1) is the most important replacement; folate, B12, and pyridoxine should also be replaced; high-dose B vitamins with alcohol cessation lead to partial neuropathy recovery in majority within 3-6 months

output.summary: IV thiamine urgently required (thiamine 28 nmol/L severely low). Folate 5 mg daily, B12 supplementation if needed (low-normal B12 228), multivitamin B complex. Alcohol cessation is the primary disease-modifying intervention. Partial neuropathy improvement expected in 3-6 months with thiamine repletion and cessation.

output.proposed: Neuropathic pain management in alcoholic neuropathy with liver disease
warnings: Gabapentin — sedation may be additive with alcohol use; preferred over tricyclics given liver disease
Avoid tricyclic antidepressants (amitriptyline) — hepatically metabolized, arrhythmia risk
Avoid duloxetine at standard doses given elevated LFTs — reduce dose or defer until liver normalizes
Acetaminophen use with care — hepatic toxicity in liver disease (max 2g/day in liver disease)
NSAIDs contraindicated — risk of GI bleed with portal hypertension
alternatives: Gabapentin 300 mg TID — start low given alcohol sedation risk
Topical lidocaine or capsaicin for localized pain

key_reasoning_points: Severe thiamine deficiency (28 nmol/L) is the most urgent finding — Wernicke encephalopathy must be prevented with immediate IV thiamine
Alcoholic-nutritional neuropathy is the primary diagnosis: alcohol 8-10 beers/day x 15 years, severe thiamine deficiency, macrocytic anemia
Alcoholic liver disease markers (AST:ALT >2, GGT 342, splenomegaly) indicate advanced hepatic disease — affects medication choices
Neuropathy prognosis: partial recovery with thiamine repletion and alcohol cessation over 3-6 months
